q: A deep laceration on the lateral mid-upper arm results in dropped wrist. Which nerve is injured in the spiral groove?
ex: Radial nerve winds around the humeral spiral groove; its lesion gives wrist drop.

q: A lymphangiogram confirms the thoracic duct. Its termination is best described at which site?
o: Junction of left internal jugular and left subclavian veins
Confluence of the two brachiocephalic veins
ex: Thoracic duct drains into the left venous angle, where the left IJV meets the left subclavian vein.

q: Which nerve supplies the short head of the biceps femoris muscle?
ex: Short head of biceps femoris sole posterior-thigh muscle supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve; the rest by the tibial.

q: All of the following are contents of the spermatic cord EXCEPT:
ex: Ilioinguinal nerve accompanies the cord along the canal but is not one of its contents.

q: The cricothyroid muscle is innervated by which of the following?
ex: Both bellies honly cricothyroid is served by the external laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

q: Which structure pierces through the diaphragma sellae of the dura mater?
ex: The infundibulum passes by the tiny opening in the diaphragma sellae roof of the pituitary fossa.

q: Within the free edge of the lesser omentum, which element of the portal triad lies the most posterior?
ex: Postero-lateral: CBD anterior, hepatic artery anteromedial, portal vein posterior-most in the omentum's free border.

q: Pain from the gallbladder inflammation is located at dermatome at the level of the umbilicus. Which spinal cord dermatome is this?
ex: Umbilicus = T10 dermatome; a standard landmark for cutaneous anesthesia boundaries.

q: A man cannot dorsiflex the ankle and drops the foot while walking. The lesion most likely involves the:
ex: Foot drop results from common fibular (peroneal) nerve palsy — its deep fibular branch dorsiflexes.

q: The inferior vena cava is formed by the union of the two common iliac veins at which vertebral level?
ex: IVC is formed at L5, to the right side of the aorta, before ascending the retroperitoneum.

q: The posterior clinoid process is a part of which bone?
ex: Sella turcica recesses — anterior and posterior clinoid processes belong to the body of the sphenoid.

q: What dermatome is the male nipple located at?
ex: Nipple level = T4 dermatome; a reference board landmark alongside umbilicus T10.

q: In epistaxis, which site in the adult nasal cavity is most commonly the source of bleeding?
ex: Most adult epistaxis is anterior from Little's area over the antero-inferior septum (Kiesselbach's plexus).

q: In a woman in her 30s with slowly progressive conductive deafness, intact tympanic membrane and a family history of similar hearing loss, the underlying pathology that has produced the blocking is:
o: Fixation of the stapes footplate in the oval window
Erosion of the incus long process
ex: Otosclerosis: overgrowth and fixation of the stapedial footplate causes conductive hearing loss, commoner in middle-aged women.

q: A pearl-white desquamating mass is seen behind an intact tympanic membrane in a patient with long-standing CSOM. The mass is produced by which tissue invading the middle ear?
ex: Cholesteatoma is an 'epithelial cyst' formed by keratinizing squamous epithelium with desquamation causing pressure erosion and discharge.

q: A teenage boy presents with recurrent severe epistaxis and progressive unilateral nasal obstruction since 3 months. Endoscopy reveals a reddish vascular lobulated mass in the posterior nasal cavity. Diagnosis?
ex: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a highly vascular, testosterone-dependent tumor classically seen in adolescent males.

q: Which is the most common benign neoplasm of the major salivary glands?
ex: Pleomorphic adenoma (mixed salivary tumor) is the most common benign tumor of the parotid and all salivary glands.

q: A 6-year-old with acute sore throat and fever has tonsillar erythema and exudates with petechiae on the palate. The most important bacterial cause here is:
ex: Acute tonsillitis is most commonly viral, but Group A beta-adrenergic hemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes is the key bacterial cause.

q: The most common site of origin of laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma is:
ex: Glottic carcinoma is the most common laryngeal cancer and presents early with hoarseness.

q: Recurrent attacks of vertigo, tinnitus and fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss with aural fullness reach us to due to:
o: Endo-lymphatic hydrops of the inner ear
An acousticic neuroma in the IAC
ex: Meniere's disease is caused by endolymphatic hydrops producing intermittent vertigo, tinnitus and fluctuating hearing loss.

q: Short-lasting vertigo induced by positional change and reproducible by the dir-Hallpike maneuver is best treated initially with:
ex: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (posterior canal BPPV) responds to the Epley canal repositioning maneuver.

q: A 3-year-old, choking, drooling, anxious, febrile and 'thumb sign' on the lateral neck radiograph is present. Causative organism?
ex: Acute epiglottitis (supraglottitis) is due to Haemophilus influenzae type b; lateral neck X-ray shows the thumb print sign; airway emergency.

q: A 34-year-old man with progressive right facial nerve weakness and for tinnitus, the MRI reveals a mass at the CP angle. The most common tumor of the cerebelloβpons:
ex: Vestibular schwannoma is the most common tumor of the internal auditory canal and the cerebello-pont angle.

q: Which facial bone is fractured with the greatest frequency after blunt maxillofacial trauma?
ex: The nasal bones are the most commonly fractured facial bone because of their central vulnerable projection.

q: A 9-month-old boy presents with recurrent early-morning (fasting) hypoglycemia, massive hepatomegaly, and a doll-like face with full cheeks. Laboratory workup shows lactic acidemia, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia. Deficiency of which enzyme is responsible?
ex: Von Gierke disease (GSD Ia) is caused by glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency; fasting hypoglycemia + hepatomegaly + hyperuricemia + dyslipidemia.

q: A 40-year-old man reports urine that turns black on standing. Examination shows dark pigment in the pinna of the ear and grayish-blue discoloration of the sclera. Radiographs of the spine reveal calcification of the intervertebral discs. The urinary pigment is homogentisic acid. Which enzyme is deficient?
ex: Alcaptonuria is due to homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency causing ochronosis with dark urine and cartilage pigmentation.

q: Which of the following is NOT a ketone body?
ex: Ketone bodies are acetoacetate, 3-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone; acetyl-CoA is their precursor, not a ketone body.

q: A newborn develops marked hyperammonemia within the first 48 hours of life with respiratory alkalosis, then vomiting and lethargy progressing to encephalopathy. Plasma citrulline is low and orotic acid is markedly elevated. The most likely enzyme deficiency is in which disorder of the urea cycle?
ex: OTC deficiency is the most common urea cycle disorder, X-linked, with hyperammonemia, low citrulline, and high orotic acid.

q: A child presents with swollen bleeding gums, petechiae over the lower limbs, and failure to heal wounds. A scorbutic rosary is seen on the chest. Deficiency of this vitamin cofactor impairs hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen synthesis.
ex: Scurvy results from ascorbic acid deficiency; vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase in collagen maturation.

q: Malonate is a structural analogue of succinate and is classically described as a competitive inhibitor of which enzyme of the TCA cycle?
ex: Malonate competes with succinate for succinate dehydrogenase, the TCA flavoprotein that also serves as complex II of the ETC.

q: A 60-year-old man presents with retrosternal chest pain. Serial troponins are elevated and ECG shows new ST elevation. Among the LDH isoenzymes, which fraction shows predominant elevation with a characteristic flipped pattern relative to its usual serum distribution?
ex: Myocardial infarction causes LDH1>LDH2 flipped pattern because cardiac muscle is rich in H-isoenzyme subunits.

q: A sample containing a mixture of serum proteins is subjected to SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis. Separation of the proteins in this technique occurs based primarily on which property?
ex: SDS coats proteins with uniform negative charge, so SDS-PAGE resolves proteins primarily by molecular mass.

q: Skeletal muscle cannot release free glucose into the blood from its glycogen stores. Which enzyme is absent in muscle, whereas present in liver and kidney, accounting for this?
ex: Liver contains glucose-6-phosphatase to liberate free glucose; muscle lacks it, so its glycogen is used for glycolysis only.

q: During DNA replication, short single-stranded DNA segments are synthesized discontinuously on the strand whose template direction is antiparallel to the advancing replication fork. These fragments are named after which discoverer and are located on which strand?
ex: Okazaki fragments are short segments synthesized on the lagging strand and later joined by DNA ligase.

q: A neonate has a mousy (musty) odour to the urine, fair skin, eczema, and microcephaly. Serum phenylalanine is markedly raised (30 mg/dL). Which enzyme is deficient?
ex: Classical PKU is deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, causing phenylalanine accumulation, musty/uratic odour, and intellectual disability if untreated.

q: A 35-year-old woman presents with fatigue, a beef-red tongue, paresthesias, and difficulty walking. Imaging shows increased T2 signal in the posterior and lateral columns of the spinal cord. Peripheral smear shows macrocytic anemia with hyperorthochromic. Deficiency of which vitamin is the cause?
ex: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megalobankism plus subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord; folate is withheld when neurologic disease present.

q: Which beta-blocker possesses intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA) and is therefore non-selective?
ex: Pindolol is the non-selective beta-blocker with partial agonist (ISA) activity; the other three have no ISA.

q: Long-term amiodarone therapy is classically associated with which adverse effect?
ex: Amiodarone's hallmark chronic toxicity is pulmonary fibrosis, alongside corneal microdeposits and thyroid dysfunction.

q: The lipid-lowering action of atorvastatin is mediated by which mechanism?
o: Blockade of the enteric MTP transporter
ex: Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step of hepatic cholesterol synthesis.

q: Which oral antidiabetic drug carries a significant risk of lactic acidosis and must be avoided when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min?
ex: Metformin, a biguanide, causes lactic acidosis, especially in renal impairment, contrast CT contrast, and hypoxemia.

q: Which antiepileptic drug most commonly causes SIADH with resultant water intoxication and hyponatremia?
ex: Carbamazepine causes SIADH; patients on chronic therapy need monitoring of serum sodium.

q: A patient on anti-tubercular therapy develops red-green color blindness. Which drug is responsible?
ex: Ethambutol causes retrobulbar optic neuritis presenting as red-green color blindness; dose-linked and reversible.

q: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) supplementation is specifically added to REGIMEN to prevent peripheral neuropathy caused by which drug?
ex: Isoniazid depletes pyridoxine, causing peripheral neuropathy; pyridoxine 10-25 mg/day prevents it.

q: What is the drug of choice for severe and complicated falciparum malaria, including cerebral malaria?
ex: IV artesunate is first-line for severe falciparum malaria; chloroquine and primaquine have no role there.

q: Which drug is used to prevent eclamptic seizures in women with severe preeclampsia?
ex: IV/IM toc Only by MgSO4 ID9 not anticonvulsant; prevents eclamptic convulsions and also treats convulsions.

q: Which drug is given to reverse the muscarinic manifestations (bradycardia, bronchoconstriction, salivation) of acute organophosphate poisoning?
ex: Atropine (IV) promptly reverses muscarinic signs; pralidoxime is adjunctive to reactivate cholinesterase.

q: A toddler accidentally ingests an overdose of ferrous sulfate and presents with vomiting and metabolic acidosis. Which agent is used for chelation of iron?
ex: Deferoxamine chelates trivalent iron; diagnostic rose-red ('vin rose') urine occurs with iron elimination.

q: Which antidote is used for life-threatening digoxin toxicity manifested by hyperkalemia and ventricular tachyarrhythmias?
ex: Digoxin immune Fab (anti-digoxin antibody) neutralizes the glycoside; atropine/lidocaine are only supportive.

q: In a body examined after death, muscles stiffen progressively. Rigor mortis is earliest appreciated in which muscle group?
ex: Rigor mortis follows Nysten's law: appears first in facial (eyelids, jaw) muscles within 1-3 hr, spreads downward, and disappears in reverse order.

q: Lividity in a body recovered from hanging is characteristically maximal over which parts, helping confirm the suspended posture?
ex: In hanging, postmortem lividity develops in dependent lower limbs and forearms (posterior parts of body stay pale from contact), unlike supine-posture livor mortis.

q: A married woman dies within one year of marriage following dowry harassment by in-laws. Death by poisoning as a result of dowry demand is prosecuted under which provision?
ex: Dowry death (within 7 yrs of marriage, cruelty/dowry demand shortly before) is abated under Sec 304B IPC; presumption of culpability against the husband applies.

q: In a long-decomposed drowning death where soft tissues are lost, which tissue should be sampled for diatom confirmation of antemortem submersion?
ex: Diatoms protect inside skull—femoral/sternal bone marrow intact gives positive diatom tests in putrefied and skeletal drowning cases.

q: A person sustains an accidental domestic electric injury. The characteristic skin lesion at the point of electrical contact is which of the following?
o: Pale grey-white, sunken well-circumscribed mark with slightly raised margin
Ghoul blackened eschar with deep charring
ex: 'Electric mark' (Marcus/current mark) is a dry, pale grey-white, depressed, well-defined lesion with raised borders; differentiating it from flame burns.

q: A man develops diffuse loss of scalp hair about 2-3 weeks after alleged poisoning, accompanied by abdominal pain and transverse white bands over the nails. Which poison is suspected?
ex: Thallium (characteristic total alopecia in 2nd-3rd week, Mees' nail stripes, retrosternal pain) is the high-yield chronic poisoning clue.

q: A worker with recurrent abdominal colic shows a blue-black discoloration along the gum margins. This enseigne is due to chronic poisoning with which heavy metal?
ex: Burton's line — a blue-black deposit along the gingival margin from lead sulfide — is pathognonomic of chronic lead poisoning.

q: The bright pink-red colour seen in the skin and mucous membranes of a person found dead inside a close room with a burnt coal brazier points to poisoning with which gas?
ex: Cherry pink symbol./mucosa = carboxyhaemoglobin (CO poisoning) — a classic internal medicine character; the red blood remains fluid for long.

q: A charred body is recovered with arms flexed and fingers clenched in a 'pugilistic attitude'. What explains this postmortem posture?
o: Heat coagulation of muscle proteins producing rigidity
Resolution of blood-liquid degeneration in the heat
ex: Heat rigor: coagulation of muscle proteins by intense heat stiffens flexors into the boxer 'pugilistic' stance, even in completely w unbalanced contexts (searching).

q: When biochemical estimation of time since death is attempted, which analyte in which fluid is most reliable for a reasonable post-mortem interval?
ex: Vitreous potassium almost immediately postmortem (~0.17-0.15 mEq/L/hr) is the meritorious biochemical marker for time since death.

q: In a cut-throat victim with a single gaping fatal cut, a cluster of short superficial parallel cuts beside the fatal wound represent what?
ex: Multiple shallow superficial 'hesitation' or 'tentative' cuts alongside deep incised wounds suggest suicide rather than homicide in throat cut deaths.

q: During a medicolegal autopsy, the standard incision on the body surface that joins the two should to the chest and abdomen is which shape?
ex: The classic autopsy 'Y-incision' runs from each shoulder to glide down to the xiphisternum (linear abdomen) — the default opening a forensic pathologist uses.

q: Leukocoria in a 2-year-old child. Most common primary intraocular malignant tumour at this age?
ex: Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood; melanoma is the most common adult one.

q: Slit-lamp shows a brownish-green ring at the peripheral cornea in a patient with tremors and elevated serum copper. Which corneal layer is involved?
ex: Kayser-Fleischer ring = copper deposition in Descemet's membrane at the limbus, pathognomonic of Wilson disease.

q: Sudden painless vision loss in one eye; fundus shows a whitened oedematous retina with a bright red fovea. Diagnosis?
ex: Cherry-red spot + retinal whitening is a central retinal artery occlusion; CRVOS shows diffuse retinal haemorrhages.

q: Bilateral small, irregular pupils that do not react to light but constrict on accommodation. Likely aetiology?
ex: Argyll Robertson pupils show light-near dissociation and are classic in neurosyphilis.

q: In an attack of acute primary angle-closure glaucoma, which drug is contraindicated?
ex: Atropine is an anticholinergic mydriatic that aggravates angle crowding; the other three drugs are used in acute angle-closure.

q: Milky-white lens with raised pressure and open angle in a 70-year-old. Diagnosis?
ex: Phacolytic glaucoma: escaping lens protein from a hypermature cataract closes the trabecular filtration.

q: Corneal ulcer advancing with an undermined liquefied edge and hypopyon. Likely organism?
ex: Ulcus serpens is the classic pneumococcal creeping ulcer with undermining edge and hypopyon.

q: Tall young man with long limbs and ectopia lentis. Commonest direction of lens displacement?
ex: Marfan syndrome subluxates the lens upward-outward; homocystinuria displaces it downward-inward.

q: Progressive night blindness with constricting peripheral fields; retina has bone-spicule pigment. Diagnosis?
ex: Bone-spicule pigment, nyctalopia and waxy disc are hallmarks of retinitis pigmentosa (rod dystrophy).

q: Right pupil paradoxically dilates when the light swings to it. Indicates?
ex: Swinging flashlight test shows Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD), indicating an afferent (optic nerve) defect.

q: Antinuclear-antibody-positive oligoarticular JIA, chronic uveitis. A classic late corneal complication is?
ex: JIA-associated uveitis is often asymptomatic and ultimately tears band-shaped keratopathy.

q: Retinal detachment caused by a full-thickness break allowing liquefied vitreous beneath the retina. Type?
ex: Rhegmatogenous is the most common detachment: a tear lets liquefied vitreous under the retina.

q: At the light-microscope level, the earliest reversible morphological change of a cell injury is
ex: Cellular swelling is the earliest reversible change; nuclear pyknosis/karyolysis marks irreversible injury.

q: A tissue section stained with Congo red shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light. The deposited material is:
ex: Congo red with apple-green birefringence under polarised light is diagnostic of amyloidosis.

q: Following arterial occlusion, which of the following organs characteristically shows liquefactive rather than coagulative necrosis?
ex: Brain infarcts are usually microscopic liquefactive; kidney, spleen and liver show coagulative necrosis.

q: Which of the following is the characteristic histologic finding of sarcoidosis?
o: Caseating granuloma with Langhans giant cells
Noncaseating epithelioid granuloma, often termed 'naked' with sparse lymphocytes
Granuloma with heavy neutrophilic infiltration only
ex: Sarcoidosis = noncaseating, berry-like epithelioid granuloma (Schaumann/asteroid bodies); tuberculosis is caseating.

q: AA (secondary) amyloidosis complicating a chronic inflammatory disease results from tissue deposition of:
ex: AA amyloid = serum amyloid A (acute-phase reactant) in RA/TB; AL = light chains, ATTR = transthyretin.

q: The Reed-Sternberg cells of classical Hodgkin lymphoma typically show which immune phenotype?
o: CD15 positive, CD30 positive and CD45 negative
ex: Reed-Sternberg cells: CD15+/CD30+ with CD45−; the owl-eye megakaryocyte-like nucleoli are classic.

q: A young adult presents with spherocytes on peripheral smear and markedly increased osmotic fragility of red cells. The most likely diagnosis is:
ex: HS: spectrin/ankyrin | defects → sphere-erythrocytes that hemolyze; osmotic fragility is increased.

q: A 5-year-old boy has nephrotic syndrome; renal biopsy on light microscope shows no abnormality but electron microscope reveals diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes. Diagnosis:
ex: Minimal change disease affects children, light microscopy normal, EM shows effacement; steroid-responsive.

q: A patient with acute promyelocytic leukemia (FAB M3) and disseminated intravascular coagulation has which cytogenetic hallmark?
ex: APL M3 → t(15;17) PML-RARA; ATRA arrenge; associated DIC due to procoagulant granules.

q: In the development of an atherosclerotic plaque, the majority of foam cells are derived from which cell type?
ex: Foam cells are lipid-laden macrophages (with some smooth muscle cells); hall of intimal atherosclerotic plaque.

q: Vitamin K-mediated carboxylation of glutamic acid residues on which coagulation zymogen produces the unusual amino acid that enables Ca2+-dependent membrane binding?
o: All proteins C and S only
Factors II, VII, IX and X not requiring carboxylation
γ-carboxyglutamic acid is generated on factors II, VII, IX, X, protein C and S
ex: Vitamin K carboxylase → glutamic → γ-carboxyglutamic acid for Ca-dependent anionic phospholipid binding.

q: A 60-year-old with a lung mass histology consistent with squamous cell carcinoma presents with hypercalcemia. The tumor paraneoplastic mediator is most likely:
ex: Squamous cell lung carcinoma produces PTHrP (not PTH) causing hypercalcemia; SCLC favors ADH/ACTH syndromes.

q: Which of the following shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the RIGHT (towards lower oxygen affinity)?
ex: Right shift produced by increased temperature, increased 2,3-DPG, increased CO2 (and reduced pH); alkalosis and cold/hypothermia shift left.

q: During the Hamburger (chloride) shift in CO2 transport, chloride enters the red blood cell in exchange for which ion released into the plasma?
ex: HCO3- generated inside RBC by carbonic anhydrase diffuses out and chloride moves in to maintain electroneutrality.

q: In a healthy adult with glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure 60 mmHg, plasma colloid osmotic pressure 30 mmHg and Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure 20 mmHg, the effective (net) filtration pressure is about:
ex: Net filtration pressure = Glomerular capillary hydrostatic − (plasma oncotic + capsular hydrostatic) ≈ 60 − (30+20) = 10 mmHg.

q: A sudden expansion of blood volume is countered mainly by release of which cardiac hormone that promotes natriuresis and vasodilation?
ex: Atrial myocytes release ANP on stretch; it antagonizes RAAS, promotes excretion of sodium and water.

q: The greatest physiological delay in impulse conduction from the atria to the ventricles occurs within:
ex: AV nodal delay (~0.1 s) allows time for ventricular filling after atrial contraction.

q: The resting membrane potential of a normal human skeletal muscle fibre is approximately:
ex: RMP of skeletal muscle about -90 mV, dominated by potassium equilibrium potential.

q: On the one that increases ventricular end-diastolic volume up to a physiological limit and thereby augments the strength of the following contraction is described by:
ex: Frank-Starling law: force of contraction increases with preload (end-diastolic und length).

q: Glomerular filtration rate is maintained nearly constant over the mean arterial pressure range of:
ex: Autoregulation keeps GFR stable when MAP between 60 and 180 mmHg, beyond this range GFR changes linearly.

q: The largest capacitance reservoir vessels holding the majority of the circulatory blood volume in the resting state are the:
ex: Veins store about 60% of total circulating blood and are termed capacitance vessels.

q: Pulmonary surfactant that prevents alveolar collapse in the new-born is synthesized by:
ex: Surfactant is produced by type II pneumocytes; deficiency causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (atelectasis).

q: In an adult, most of the erythropoietin that drives red cell production is synthesised by cells in the:
ex: Peritubular per papillary cells of kidney make ~90% of EPO, detected by hypoxia; in fetal life liver contributes more.

q: In whole blood with a total carrying capacity about 20 mL O2/dL at saturation, the largest fraction of the oxygen is transported as:
o: Oxise oxygen bound to hemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin
ex: About 97% of transported O2 is bound to hemoglobin; only ~1.5% is physically dissolved.

q: A state is planning a community survey using two-stage cluster random sampling. The required sample size computed by simple random sampling formula should be inflated by a factor of approximately:
ex: Cluster sampling loses statistical precision vs simple random sampling; multiply by the design effect (about 2), the classic EPI/30-cluster rule.

q: A designated network of sentinel hospitals voluntarily reports weekly influenza-like illness to the surveillance system. This type of monitoring is called:
ex: Sentinel surveillance uses voluntarily participating, designated sites/hospitals; passive relies on routine reporting, active involves field-worker contact with the population.

q: Among the following vaccines in the Universal Immunization Program cold chain, which is the MOST thermolabile:
ex: OPV (Sabin live-attenuated) is the most heat-sensitive UIP vaccine; a reconstituted ampoule must be used within the day and discarded if not.

q: A child in rural North India presents with acute febrile encephalopathy in monsoon; IgM-capture ELISA is positive. Which mosquito transmits this infection?
ex: Japanese encephalitis virus is transmitted by Culex tritaeniorhynchus; pigs and pond herons act as amplifier hosts.

q: For India to declare elimination of Kala-azar at block level, the annual incidence target is less than:
ex: Kala-azar elimination target: less than 1 case per 10,000 population per year at block level.

q: WHO and UNICEF (2004) recommended replacing standard ORS with a reduced-osmolarity formulation whose sodium concentration is:
ex: Reduced-osmolarity ORS: sodium 75 mEq/L, glucose 75, total osmolarity ~245 mOsm/L.

q: In a coronary artery disease cohort: 20/100 exposed smokers became ill vs 5/100 non-smokers over one decade. Attributable risk per 100 exposed is:
ex: Attributable risk = risk(exposed) − risk(unexposed) = 20 − 5 = 15 per 100.

q: In a randomized trial, several subjects cross over or stop their assigned intervention. Analysis of all subjects according to the group to which they were originally randomized is called:
ex: Intention-to-treat: analyze everyone in their randomized category irrespective of adherence; preserves randomization balance and minimizes selection bias.

q: The chief feature of Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK) is:
o: Institutional delivery cash transfer to BPL mothers
Absolutely free delivery and free care for sick newborns up to 30 days in public facilities
Free ambulance for all emergency obstetric cases
Free Nutri-kit for six months after delivery
ex: This fatality targets zero-expense delivery: free drugs, diagnostics, diet, transport for pregnant women and sick neonates up to 30 days in public hospitals.

q: The National Family Health Survey NFHS-5 followed NFHS-4, and its main fieldwork was conducted during:
ex: NFHS-5 phasewise fieldwork 2019-21, provides district-level data on fertility, mortality and welfare indicators.

q: A sudden surge of fever, retro-orbital pain with rash and thrombocytopenia in an urban area is attributed to dengue. The vector is:
ex: Aedes aegypti transmits dengue; urban, day-biting, breeding in clean stored water.

q: As per the Universal Immunization Program (UIP), the OPV birth dose (OPV-0) should be given within how many days of birth?
ex: OPV-0 birth dose should be given within the first 15 days of life (polio vaccination window).

q: A 60-year-old man presents with painless, progressively deepening jaundice and a distended, palpable gallbladder. Which condition best explains these findings?
o: Carcinoma of the head of pancreas
ex: Courvoisier's law: painless jaundice with an enlarged palpable gallbladder points to malignant obstruction (e.g., carcinoma head of pancreas), not gallstones.

q: During examination a hernia is found to protrude through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. Which type of hernia is this?
ex: Direct inguinal hernias emerge through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels; indirect ones travel lateral to them alongside the cord.

q: A 40-year-old man with a history of diarrhoea has fever and tenderness in the right upper quadrant. USG shows a single well-defined collection in the right lobe of the liver; aspiration yields pus resembling anchovy sauce. What is the most likely causative organism?
ex: Anchovy-sauce (chocolate-brown) pus and right-lobe liver abscess are classic amebic liver abscess; pyogenic abscesses do not have this appearance.

q: A 20-year-old man complains of RIF pain that now extends to the thigh and worsening on extension of the right hip (psoas sign positive). Which anatomical position of the appendix best explains this sign?
ex: A positive psoas sign indicates an inflamed retrocaecal appendix overlying the psoas muscle, causing pain on hip extension.

q: Two days after a total thyroidectomy for carcinoma, a patient complains of persistent hoarseness of voice. Which injury best explains this presentation?
o: Injury to the external laryngeal nerve
ex: Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis causes hoarseness; bilateral injury causes stridor and airway obstruction.

q: A 60-year-old man has a firm painless lump in the breast with skin retraction. Excisional biopsy is ordered. Which histopathological type is the most common breast malignancy in men?
ex: Invasive ductal carcinoma accounts for the majority (~85%) of male breast cancers; lobular and other subtypes are rare in men.

q: A 17-year-old boy has acute severe left scrotal and lower abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The left testis is high-riding with absent cremasteric reflex and a diffusely tender hemiscrotum. What is the diagnosis?
ex: High-lying testis with absent cremasteric reflex in acute pain = torsion; a surgical emergency needing detorsion within hours.

q: A 55-year-old man with underlying cirrhosis and portal hypertension presents with painless hematemesis and melena. Which esophageal cause is the most common source of bleeding?
ex: Variceal bleeding is the most common cause of upper GI haemorrhage in cirrhosis from portal hypertension.

q: You need to quickly choose an approximate TBSA for a small burn wound in an adult. Using the 'patient's palm' method, what percentage is one palm including the fingers taken as approximately equal to?
ex: The patient's own palm with fingers approximates 1% of TBSA, useful for small and irregular burns.

q: A patient who had a partial gastrectomy two years ago develops sweating, palpitations, and weakness with confusion about 2 hours after a heavy carbohydrate meal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Late dumping occurs 1–3 hours post-meal from reflex hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia; early dumping is a rapid gastric emptying effect within 30 minutes.

q: A 70-year-old man presents with colicky pain, abdominal distension, and constipation of 3 days with features of large bowel obstruction. Plain films confirm a dilated right colon. Which is the most common underlying cause in an adult?
ex: Colorectal carcinoma is the commonest cause of large bowel obstruction in adults; a mechanical cause must be excluded first.

q: A 30-year-old man with painful defecation and a sentinel at a posterior midline site. Which is the characteristic location of the most common anal fissure in adults?
o: Posterior midline of the anal canal
Anterior midline of the anal canal ture
Lateral wall of the anal canal
ex: In adults the typical fissure-in-ano is midline, classically posteriorly (the anal pressure is maximal here), sentinel pile taking it chronic.

q: Stool from a suspected cholera patient yields large smooth yellow colonies on TCBS agar. Which organism is responsible?
ex: Vibrio cholerae ferments sucrose, giving yellow colonies on TCBS agar; TCBS is the selective medium of choice for cholera.

q: A research scientist wishes to cultivate Mycobacterium leprae from a patient of lepromatous leprosy. Which experimental host must be used, as the organism cannot grow on artificial media?
ex: Mycobacterium leprae cannot be cultured on artificial media; it grows only in the mouse footpad (and nine-banded armadillo).

q: A rice-field worker presents with high fever, myalgia and conjunctival suffusion. Fresh blood is examined by which method for the causative spirochaete?
ex: Leptospira is detected by dark-field microscopy of fresh blood (or urine) in early leptospirosis.

q: An infant develops descending flaccid paralysis and difficulty breathing after consuming contaminated honey. What is the mechanism of the toxin responsible?
o: Competes with choline for presynaptic reuptake
ex: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release, causing flaccid paralysis.

q: A hospitalized patient on broad-spectrum antibiotics develops severe pseudomembranous colitis. Which selective medium is used to isolate the causative organism?
ex: Clostridioides difficile is isolated on CCFA, a selective medium for anaerobic gram-positive rods.

q: Which animals are the natural reservoir for lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus and Lassa virus, the two arenaviruses of human importance?
ex: Arenaviruses (Lassa, LCM) are rodent-borne; humans acquire infection by contact with rodent excreta.

q: A child with watery diarrhea is found to have the causative virus showing a wheel-like appearance on electron microscopy of stool. Which virus is it?
ex: Rotavirus is the leading cause of viral gastroenteritis in infants; 70 nm triple-layered capsid appears wheel-like on electron microscopy.

q: Which exotoxin acts by ADP-ribosylating elongation factor 2 and halting protein synthesis in the host cell?
ex: Diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates elongation factor-2, inhibiting host protein synthesis.

q: Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis has spread through a school via contaminated swarming pool water and fingers. Which virus is implicated?
ex: Enterovirus 70 (picornavirus) is the classic cause of acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis, spread via contaminated fingers and fomites.

q: Which laboratory reaction detects the presence of Clostridium perfringens by showing a zone inhibited by one formation on egg-yolk agar in the presence of antihoco, thereby pathological lecithinase?
ex: Nagler reaction alpha toxin (lecithinase) produced by Clostridium perfringens is inhibited by antiserum on egg measles, distinguishing it from other clostridia.

q: A patient is a diffuse aerobic pulmonary disease with enderness and Section pecto, that yeast-like: microscopy shows thin branching partially indistinguishable hyphae of the actin mycete. Which foot solid pathogen most likely responsible, career-acquaintanced with a why? Non-influenza, wrangservices most A known opportunistic actinomycete, not anaerobic soft tissue.
ex: Nocardia asteroides is an aerobic ray-fungus (actinomycete) that stains gram+ and partially underlying; causes pulmonary disease, most often cerebral, with sulfur granules commonly forming brain absscess.

q: The most common site of implantation of a tubal ectopic pregnancy is the:
ex: Ampulla hosts ~55% of tubal ectopics; tubal location accounts for >95% of all ectopic gestations.

q: Which karyotype is characteristic of a partial hydatidiform mole?
ex: Partial mole is triploid (two paternal haploid sets + one maternal), typically 69,XXY; complete mole is diploid 46,XX androgenetic.

q: At the moment of ovulation, the secondary oocyte is arrested at which stage of meiosis?
ex: Ovulated oocyte arrests in Metaphase II until fertilization; meiosis I already completed pre-ovulation.

q: In the two-cell/two-gonadotrophin theory of ovarian steroidogenesis, androstenedione is produced chiefly by:
ex: Theca interna (LH receptor) makes androgens; granulosa cells (FSH) aromatize them to estradiol.

q: The single most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage is:
ex: Uterine atony causes ~70-80% of PPH; exclude retained placenta and trauma before diagnosing.

q: A fibroid becomes acutely painful, tender and feverish during pregnancy. The most likely degeneration is:
ex: Red (carneous) degeneration occurs particularly in pregnancy, producing acute pain, fever and a tender mass.

q: The most common germ cell tumor of the ovary is:
ex: Mature cystic teratoma is the commonest ovarian germ cell tumor and benign; dysgerminoma is the commonest malignant germ cell.

q: Antidote for magnesium sulfate toxicity during eclampy iv therapy is:
ex: IV calcium gluconate reverses MgSO4 toxicity; monitor respiratory depression, urine output, patellar reflexes.

q: In chorioma carcinoma, the most common site of distant drainage settlement is:
ex: GTN spreads hematosisexil; lung is the most frequent metastasis (present in up to 90% of advanced disease).

q: The most common malignant germ cell tumor of the ovary is:
ex: Dysgerminoma (radiosensitive, marker-free) is the commonest malignant ovarian germ cell tumour; yolk sac is the 'shiny' LDH/AFP pattern.

q: Milk letdown during nipple suckling is mediated primarily by:
ex: Nipple stimulation triggers a neuroendocrine reflex releasing oxytocin for milk ejection; prolactin drives milk production.

q: First-line ovulation induction to a patient with anovulatory PCOS wanting pregnancy:
ex: Letrozole (aromatase inhibitor) is first-line in PCOS anovulation; clomiphene reserved as alternative, better pregnancy/labour outcome with letrozole.

q: A 24-year-old patient hears two voices conversing about him in third person, and reports that his thoughts are being broadcast to others. Which symptom is a Schneiderian first-rank symptom of schizophrenia?
o: Third-person auditory hallucinations and thought broadcast
ex: Schneiderian first-rank symptoms: third-person acoustic hallucinations, thought insertion/broadcast/withdrawal, passivity phenomena.

q: A 28-year-old on long-term haloperidol develops high fever, severe rigidity, diaphoresis, autonomic instability and serum CPK of 4200 IU/L. Most likely diagnosis?
ex: NMS: extrapyramidal rigidity + hyperthermia + autonomic instability + raised CPK after high-potency typical antipsychotics; stop drug, supportive care, dantrolene/bromocriptine.

q: A chronic alcoholic develops severe amnesia with fabrication of events he insists are true. Which feature most characterizes this condition?
ex: Korsakoff psychosis = thiamine (B1) deficiency with anterograde amnesia + confabulation, sequel of Wernicke encephalopathy.

q: Which endocrine disturbance is a known long-term complication of lithium maintenance therapy?
ex: Lithium blocks ADH action at renal V2/D2-receptors causing nephrogenic DI; monitor lithium levels, nephrotoxic interaction with NSAIDs.

q: An ICU patient abruptly develops fluctuation in attention and level of consciousness over hours. Which feature is hallmark of delirium that best distinguishes it from dementia?
ex: Delirium = acute onset, fluctuating attention/level of consciousness; the core diagnostic hallmark is inattention.

q: A patient on long-term typical antipsychotic develops repeated lip-smacking, tongue protrusion and grimacing. Which region is most commonly involved in tardive dyskinesia?
ex: Tardive dyskinesia most often affects orofacial muscles (lip-smacking, tongue protrusion); switch to clozapine if severe.

q: A chronic alcoholic admitted for treatment develops confusion, fever, hallucinations and tremors. At which time interval after last drink does delirium tremens typically peak?
ex: DT peaks at 48-72 h after withdrawal (seizures at 24-48 h); mortality up to 20% untreated; manage with benzodiazepines.

q: A 22-year-old with contamination obsessions and washing compulsions is started on pharmacotherapy. Which class is first-line for OCD?
ex: SSRIs (fluoxetine/sertraline/fluvoxamine/escitalopram) are first-line for OCD, usually at higher doses, along with CBT.

q: A patient on fluoxetine develops fever, agitation, myoclonus, hyperreflexia and diarrhea after starting another five-drug regimen. Most likely diagnosis?
ex: Serotonin syndrome: serotonergic excess (SSRI + MAOI/linezolid/meperidine) — mental status change + autonomic hyperactivity + neuromuscular (clonus); discontinue agents, give cyproheptadine.

q: A young woman with bulimia nervosa self-induces vomiting and has callosities over the dorsum of her dominant hand. This finding is called:
ex: Russell's sign = callosities/abrasions on dorsum of hand from repeated self-induced vomiting in bulimia nervosa.

q: A few hours after receiving a depot antipsychotic, a patient develops eye deviation, opisthotonos and torticollis. Drug of choice?
ex: Acute dystonia from antipsychotics responds rapidly to anticholinergics (benztropine/diphenhydramine) IM/IV.

q: A 40-year-old woman avoids markets, buses and crowds for a fear she cannot escape or receive help, and now rarely leaves home. Diagnosis?
ex: Agoraphobia = anxiety about public/open situations where escape/falling may be difficult; commonly comorbid with panic disorder.

q: A 45-year-old woman with menorrhagia and a strict vegetarian diet has Hb 8.2 g/dL and MCV 88 fL. The peripheral smear shows a dimorphic picture with both macrocytes and microcytic hypochromic cells. Which combination of deficiencies best explains this pattern?
o: Folate plus iron deficiency with thalassemia trait
ex: Combined iron + B12 deficiency masks each other's effect on MCV - the smear is dimorphic and MCV may read normal.

q: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes is being treated for diabetic ketoacidosis. Below which serum potassium level (mmol/L) must insulin be withheld and potassium replaced first?
ex: Insulin drives K+ intracellularly - in DKA start insulin only when serum K+ is above 3.3 mmol/L to prevent fatal hypokalemia.

q: A 68-year-old woman with Graves disease has fever, tachycardia and agitation suggestive of thyroid storm. Which drug both blocks thyroid hormone synthesis and inhibits peripheral T4 to T3 conversion, and is therefore preferred to rapidly lower circulating T3?
ex: Propylthiouracil inhibits type 1 deiodinase (T4 to T3) in addition to synthesis - the drug of choice in thyroid storm.

q: A young injection-drug user has fever, a new murmur and an oscillating mass on the mitral valve at echocardiography. According to the Duke criteria for infective endocarditis, which of the following is a MAJOR criterion?
o: Echocardiographic vegetation or new valvular regurgitation
ex: Duke major criteria: positive blood cultures for a typical organism and echocardiographic evidence of new vegetation - fever and skin lesions are minor criteria.

q: In a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus, which autoantibody is most specific for renal involvement and is the standard test to monitor disease activity in lupus nephritis?
ex: Anti-dsDNA is SLE-specific, correlates with nephritis and mirrors disease activity; it is used for monitoring.

q: A 55-year-old man has crushing retrosternal pain for 40 minutes. Which electrocardiographic finding is the EARLIEST to appear in the evolution of STEMI?
ex: Hyperacute peaked T waves appear within minutes of coronary occlusion, before ST elevation; Q waves appear much later.

q: A patient on isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol develops hepatitis in the sixth week. The hepatotoxicity of which drug is mediated chiefly by the toxic metabolite acetylhydrazine?
ex: Acetylhydrazine, a metabolite of isoniazid, is the most common cause of hepatotoxicity during anti-TB therapy.

q: A 30-year-old man has low grade fever and headache for 3 weeks and now has neck stiffness. CSF: lymphocytes 320, protein 180 mg/dL, glucose 18 mg/dL (serum 90). What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Lymphocytic pleocytosis with high protein and low glucose is classic for tuberculous meningitis; viral meningitis rarely lowers glucose.

q: In a patient with cirrhosis and ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed when the polymorphonuclear count in ascitic fluid exceeds which value?
ex: Ascitic fluid PMN greater than 250 cells/µL defines SBP and is an indication for empirical antibiotics.

q: Sofosbuvir is a backbone agent in direct-acting antiviral therapy for chronic hepatitis C. Which viral enzyme does it inhibit?
ex: Sofosbuvir is a finite nucleotide inhibitor of NS5B polymerase; glecaprevir is NS3/4A and declarator targets NS5A.

q: A patient on diuretics has serum sodium 128 mmol/L and potassium 2.8 mmol/L. Which electrocardiographic feature would you most expect in this setting?
o: Prominent U waves with flat or inverted T waves
ST-segment elevation in the precordial leads
ex: Hypokalaemia produces prominent U waves and flattened T waves, whereas tall tented T waves indicate hyperkalaemia.

q: Which of the following is NOT a component of the CURB-65 severity score for community-acquired pneumonia?
o: Respiratory rate of 30 per minute or more
ex: CURB-65 = Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, RR>=30, BP<90/60, age>=65; hypoxemia is not part of the score.

q: In a healthy full-term infant, birth weight typically doubles at approximately which age?
ex: Birth weight doubles ~5 months, triples ~1 year, quadruples ~2 years.

q: A 2-month-old infant on routine examination has a small midline gap at the junction of the lambdoid and sagittal sutures. When does this posterior fontanelle normally close?
ex: Posterior fontanelle closes by 2-3 months; anterior fontanelle by 12-18 months.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five components assessed in the Apgar score at birth?
ex: Apgar = heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability, colour; pulse oximetry is not a component.

q: A 6-year-old girl presents with dysuria and frequency. Urine culture grows >10^5 CFU/mL. Most likely causative organism of community-acquired UTI in this age group?
ex: E. coli causes about 80-90% of first/community-acquired UTIs in children.

q: A healthy term newborn is to receive prophylaxis against hemorrhagic disease of the newborn. Correct regimen?
o: Vitamin K 1 mg oral, single dose
No prophylaxis is needed in term newborns
ex: 1 mg vitamin K IM at birth prevents early classic VKDB.

q: A 4-month-old with coryza, cough and first episode of wheeze in winter; chest film shows hyperinflation. Most likely causative virus?
ex: RSV is the commonest cause of bronchiolitis, peaking in infancy winter.

q: A 4-month-old boy with progressive cyanosis and episodes of anoxic spells. Echocardiogram shows tetralogy of Fallot. Which defect is the MOST common cyanotic congenital heart disease overall?
ex: TOF is the most common cyanotic CHD; VSD is the most common CHD overall.

q: An 8-year-old develops hematuria and edema 2 weeks after an untreated sore throat. What is the typical latent period between throat infection and acute post-streptococcal GN in children?
ex: PSGN after pharyngeal infection has a latent period of 1-2 weeks; after skin infection 3-6 weeks.

q: A 9-year-old with prolonged fever, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, rash and multi-organ involvement presented 4 weeks after confirmed household COVID-19 infection. CRP strikingly elevated. Most likely diagnosis?
ex: MIS-C follows COVID-19 exposure by 4-6 weeks with fever + multi-system inflammation (often resembling Kawasaki).

q: A 3-year-old with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome, in remission, has now relapsed twice in the past 6 months. How is this pattern classified?
ex: Frequent relapse = >=2 relapses within 6 months (or >=4 per year).

q: A 5-year-old with fever, headache and vomiting for 10 days; CSF shows lymphocytes, protein 150 mg/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL. Which constellation best fits tuberculous meningitis?
o: Normal protein, low glucose, high neutrophils
ex: TBM CSF : increased protein, decreased glucose (usually <45) with lymphocytic pleocytosis.

q: A preterm newborn has a continuous machinery murmur and hyperdynamic precordium. Ductus remains hemodynamically significant. Which medication is standard for pharmacological closure in the preterm infant?
ex: Indomethacin (or ibuprofen), a COX inhibitor, is the standard first-line for symptomatic PDA closure in preterms.

q: The earliest, most sensitive monitoring sign of malignant hyperthermia during routine anaesthesia is:
ex: MH earliest sign is rising ETCO2 (hypermetabolism); treatment dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg, triggered classically by sux + halothane.

q: Which of the following existing conditions makes succinylcholine unsafe due to risk of fatal hyperkalaemia?
o: Healthy adult for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Deep burn sustained three weeks earlier
First-trimester pregnancy for emergency bowel surgery
Contained (closed) periorbital injury without raised ICP
ex: Burns >48h, crush, tetraplegia, prolonged immobility upregulate ACh receptors; sux triggers massive K+ efflux.

q: Which complication is most commonly encountered with an interscalene approach to brachial plexus block?
o: Ipsilateral phrenic nerve blockade with hemidiaphragmatic paresis
ex: Interscalene block → phrenic (C3-5) paresis most frequent; pneumothorax is the classic risk of the supraclavicular route.

q: Progressive interruption in amplitude of consecutive responses to train-of-four stimulation indicates:
ex: TOF fade is the hallmark of non-depolarising / phase II block; phase I sux shows no fade.

q: The gastric contents profile classically predicting severe acid aspiration (Mendelson's) pneumonitis is:
o: Any volume with pH 7 in a 6 h fast
Mucous content of pH 6 with volume 5 mL/kg
ex: Threshold for severe aspiration pneumonitis: volume >25 mL (≈0.4 mL/kg) and pH <2.5.

q: Induction agent of choice for an unstable patient with cardiac tamponade requiring urgent intubation:
ex: Etomidate produces least haemodynamic change in the shocked patient; single-dose transient adrenal suppression noted.

q: The MAC (minimum alveolar concentration) of nitrous oxide at 1 atmosphere is closest to:
ex: N2O MAC ≈ 104%; contrast volatile agents: halothane 0.75%, isoflurane 1.15%, sevoflurane 2%, desflurane 6%.

q: Drug that selectively and rapidly reverses a deep rocuronium-induced block:
ex: Sugammadex = γ-cyclodextrin binding rocuronium/vecuronium in a 1:1 inclusion complex, 2-16 mg/kg.

q: Which local anaesthetic is strictly contraindicated in intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier's block)?
ex: Tourniquet failure floods bupivacaine systemically → refractory cardiac arrest; prilocaine is preferred for Bier's.

q: Severe post-dural puncture headache refractory to bed rest and analgesia is best managed by:
ex: PDPH is postural (worse upright) from low ICP; definitive cure = epidural blood patch (≈20 mL).

q: Nitrous oxide anaesthesia is contraindicated in a patient who also has:
o: Pneumothorax drained by an intercostal tube
ex: N2O diffuses into air-filled cavities rapidly (pneumothorax, bowel obstruction, middle ear), even past drains.

q: Maximum recommended dose of plain lidocaine (no adrenaline) for infiltration in an adult is closest to:
ex: Plain lignocaine ceiling ≈ 4 mg/kg, raised to ≈7 mg/kg with adrenaline; bupivacaine ~1-2 mg/kg.

q: A 30-year-old woman presents with flaccid blisters of the oral mucosa and trunk that rupture easily. A Tzank smear from the blister base shows acantholytic cells. Which autoantibody is most characteristic of her disease?
ex: Pemphigus vulgaris is an intraepidermal/acantholytic disease with IgG against desmoglein 3 (mucosal) and desmoglein 1 (cutaneous).

q: A patient with PS psoriasis areas shows pinpoint bleeding that appears when the scaly surface of a plaque is scraped. What is this sign called?
ex: Auspitz sign = punctate bleeding on scaling removal, characteristic of psoriasis.

q: A 40-year-old man has intense itchy skin lines between fingers and wrists. Smear microscopy of the track region reveals a mite. Where is the classic site of involvement in adults?
o: Interdigital web spaces of the hands
ex: Scabies burrows classically in interdigital web spaces; palms never involved in adults (normal in infants).

q: A 65-year-old woman has tense blisters of skin skin and oral ulcers are absent. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear deposition of C3 and IgG along the dermo-epidermal junction. Which diagnosis fits best?
ex: Bullous pemphigoid: subepidermal with tense blisters, IIFS shows linear IgG/C3 at basement membrane (BP180/BP230).

q: A patient with fluoro toxic epidermal necrolysis has epidermal detachment affecting 35% of the body surface area. What is the correct classification of this condition?
ex: Epidermal detachment: SJS <10%, overlap 10-30%, TEN >30% of body surface area.

q: In a 45-year-old man with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches and a thickened enlarged ulnar nerve. Which leprosy type shows a characteristically negative lepromin (Mudrada) skin test?
ex: Lepromin/Mudda test positive in tuberculoid, negative in clinic lepromatous (low CMI).

q: A young man has pruritic, dark violet, polygonal, flat-topped papules limited to the flexor surface of wrists with lacy net-like white lines over the oral check mucosa. Which sign is pathognomonic?
ex: Wickham striae = reticulated of the planus pattern on lichen plan, counts on the surface of papules.

q: A 2-year-old has 6 days of fever with bilateral non-punctate conjunctive injection, cracked red lips, strawberry, and erythema his major palms with peeling during conv. Which treatment within 10 days of onset reduces coronary artery complications?
ex: IVIG 2 g/kg (with aspirin) within 10 days of fever cuts coronary aneurysm rates in Kawasaki disease from ~20% to <5%.

q: A 6-year-old child has multiple skin -colored, discrete papules 3-5 mm with a white in the sp soaked center. What infectious agent is responsible?
ex: Molluscum contagiosum is a DNA poxvirus (Molluscipoxvirus); papules with central embedding/dell.

q: A 22-year-old woman lasts ever since small solitary slightly scaly oval salmon-pink patch appears on the trunk, followed days later by multiple similar smaller eruptions distributed along the skin lines in a 'Christmas tree' pattern. What is the initial lesion called?
ex: Herald patch precedes the generalized eruption of pityriasis rosea along Langer's lines.

q: A young man has a sharply coin-shaped hairless patch of the scalp much more with broken hair stubs at its rim. The affected hairs appear clubbed and widen distally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Exclamation-mark hair (thin proximally, clubbed/distally) is a hallmark of alopecia areata.

q: A 55-year-old Indian man has a brown-black pigmented plaque with a nodule on the sole that grows over a year. Histologically shows junctional melanocyte proliferation in the lentiginous pattern. Which melanoma subtype is most common in his ethnic group?
ex: Acral lentiginous melanoma most common melanoma of palms, soles, subunguals in darker -skinned races.

q: A newborn vomiting since the first feed has a supine abdominal X-ray with a single double bubble and no distal gas. Likely diagnosis:
ex: Double bubble sign (gas in stomach + proximal duodenum) = duodenal atresia.

q: A 12-year-old boy with thigh pain has an X-ray showing a fusiform diaphyseal lesion with layered onion-peel periosteal reaction. Diagnosis:
ex: Laminated onion-skin periosteal reaction over a diaphyseal permeative lesion in a child = Ewing sarcoma.

q: Distal femur X-ray (an adolescent) shows a metaphyseal lesion with sunburst speculated periosteal reaction and a Codman triangle. Diagnosis:
ex: Sunburst periosteal reaction with Codman triangle around a metaphyseal osteoid tumor = osteosarcoma.

q: A 65-year-old man's skull radiograph shows patchy cotton wool sclerosis with an enlarged vault. Diagnosis:
ex: Cotton-wool skull with enlarged vault = Paget disease.

q: Chest X-ray of a foundry worker shows ring-like eggshell calcification of the hilar lymph nodes. Most likely cause:
ex: Eggshell calcification of hilar nodes is classic for silicosis.

q: A dyspneic patient with heart failure has a chest film showing butterfly perihilar opacity sparing the periphery. Diagnosis:
ex: Bat-wing perihilar opacities sparing the periphery = alveolar pulmonary edema.

q: Elderly patient with abdominal distension: X-ray shows a coffee-bean gas loop and enema shows a bird's beak taper. Diagnosis:
ex: Coffee-bean disblocked loop plus bird's beak at barium enema = sigmoid volvulus.

q: Supine chest X-ray of an intubated trauma patient shows an unusually lucent deep right costophrenic angle. Likely diagnosis:
ex: Deep sulcus sign = pneumothorax on a supine film.

q: Skull X-ray of a chronically anemic child shows striated perpendicular hair-on-end spicules widening the diploe. Diagnosis:
ex: Hair-on-end diploic spicules = extramedullary hematopoiesis in thalassemia major.

q: Infant with colicky pain and currant-jelly stools: right hypochondrial ultrasound shows a target ring sign. Diagnosis:
ex: Target/ay sign on US = intussusception.

q: A young woman's PA chest film shows bilateral hilar plus right paratracheal adenopathy in a 1-2-3 pattern. Most likely cause:
ex: 1-2-3 sign (both hinterval nodes + right paratracheal) = sarcoidosis.

q: Contrast-enhanced head CT shows a non-enhancing central delta wrapping a facet of the superior sagittal sinus. In post-typofrontal, fits best:
ex: Empty delta sign is a hyperene-sense acute sinus thrombosis.

q: A 45-year-old man falls on an outstretched hand and develops pain and tenderness in the anatomic snuffbox. Which carpal bone is most commonly fractured in this injury?
ex: Scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone (FOOSH injury); its retrograde blood supply puts the proximal pole at risk of AVN and non-union.

q: A 6-year-old boy falls on the elbow. X-ray shows a fracture of the proximal ulna with the radial head displaced off it. This Monteggia fracture-dislocation pattern classically dislocates which joint?
ex: Monteggia injury = fracture of the proximal third of the ulna with dislocation of the radial head; the reverse Galeazzi lesion involves a distal radius fracture with DRUJ disruption.

q: An elderly woman falls on her outstretched palm and develops a painful wrist that shows a dinner-fork-like dorsal bump. Which fracture explains this deformity?
ex: The dinner-fork (silver-fork) wrist deformity is the classic signature of a Colles-type extra-articular distal radius fracture with dorsal tilt and displacement.

q: A newborn delivered with shoulder traction keeps the arm adducted with forearm pronated, palm facing backwards ("waiter's tip"). Which cervical roots are affected in this pattern?
ex: Erb palsy = C5-C6 upper plexus lesion with waiter's-tip posture; Klumpke lower roots (C8-T1) give claw hand plus ipsilateral Horner syndrome.

q: A young adult with a traction injury develops a claw hand with an ipsilateral drooping eyelid and small pupil. Which nerve roots are involved?
ex: Klumpke palsy = lower brachial plexus roots C8-T1; involvement at T1 carries Horner syndrome along with the claw hand.

q: Two days after a closed tibial shaft fracture immobilised in a cast, the patient has intense pain not relieved by analgesia, pain on passive toe stretch and a tense calf. Which single action is most appropriate now?
o: Firmly wrap the fracture in crepe bandage for a week
Elevate the limb above heart level
Check intra-compartmental pressure as the next step
ex: Compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency diagnosed mainly clinically; tense limb plus pain on passive stretch mandates fasciotomy, not elevation or rest.

q: In children, which injury most commonly produces acute forearm compartment syndrome that may later lead to Volkmann ischemic contracture if undiagnosed?
o: Fracture of the radial head with posterior interosseous palsy
ex: In children, the supracondylar fracture of the humerus ranks highest among injuries that cause acute forearm compartment syndrome and later Volkmann ischemia contracture.

q: A 17-year-old boy has night pain and a warm swelling just above the knee. X-ray shows a sunburst pattern of subperiosteal bone formation. Which bone is the typical most frequent interface for this tumour?
ex: Osteosarcoma arises in the metaphysis around the knee, distal femur being the seat, with a sunburst of radioactive bone and Codman triangle at the margins.

q: A 30-year-old woman has mild pain and swelling at the wrist. X-ray of the distal radius end shows a radiolucent, eccentric expansile soap-bubble lesion crossing the epiphysis. Most likely diagnosis?
ex: Giant cell tumour is epimetaphyseal, eccentric and lytic with a soap-bubble look, and the most common settled site is the distal femur / proximal tibia.

q: A 15-year-old boy has a hard, painless, slow growing bony lump on the media of the proximal tibia, present for years. The X-ray shows a bone stalk continuous with the shaft. Which tumour is this?
ex: Osteochondroma is a cartilaginous-protruding bony growth anchored to the metaphysis; it stops growing at skeletal maturity and sarcomatous the cap enlarges after.

q: A 7-year-old has fever and a warm tender lower thigh refusing to bear weight. Which bone group is the most common site of acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in children?
ex: Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in children classically localises in the metaph bers of long bones around the knee (femur and tibia), at the site of the nutrient artery loops close to the growth plate.

q: A footballer pivots on the knee and the joint later feels as if it gives way. The tibia slides in front of the femur with the knee flexed. Which ligament has been torn?
ex: A positive anterior drawer test slides the tibia forward in front of the femur at 90 degrees of knee flexion, and is the classic sign of a torn anterior cruciate ligament.

q: The saccule, an otolith organ sensing gravity and linear acceleration, embryologically develops from which part of the otocyst?
ex: The saccule and cochlear duct arise from pars inferior; utricle and semicircular canals from pars superior.

q: Which eponymous reflex describes coughing when the external auditory canal is scratched or stimulated?
ex: Arnold's (alderman's) nerve is the auricular branch of the vagus innervating the EAC, producing a cough reflex.

q: A patient with stenosis of the cartilaginous external auditory canal requires a procedure to widen it. Which one is performed?
ex: Meatoplasty enlarges the cartilaginous (meatal) part of the external canal; canalplasty addresses bony canal stenosis.

q: A patient has a painless, foul-smelling ear discharge with multiple tympanic membrane perforations and pale granulations. Which classical feature of tuberculous otitis media is least typical?
o: Facial nerve paresis out of proportion
ex: Tuberculous otitis media is remarkably painless with polyperforation, pale granulation and early facial nerve palsy.

q: A patient complains of intranasal obstruction even though the nasal cavity looks abnormally wide with a roomy interior, crusted yellowish-green scales and anosmia the patient does not perceive. The most likely diagnosis is?
ex: Atrophic rhinitis gives a paradoxically roomy, crusted nose with 'merciful anosmia' to the fetid discharge.

q: Arrange in correct rostral sequence the ascending central auditory pathway: cochlear nucleus, spiral ganglion, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate body, superior olivary complex.
o: Spiral ganglion → cochlear nucleus → superior olivary → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate
Cochlear nucleus → spiral ganglion → superior olive → medial geniculate → inferior colliculus
Medial geniculate → inferior colliculus → superior olive → cochlear nucleus → spiral ganglion
Spiral ganglion → superior olive → cochlear nucleus → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate
ex: Auditory signals pass: spiral (Scarpa) ganglion → dorsal/ventral cochlear nuclei → SOC → inferior colliculus → MGB → auditory cortex (Brodmann 41).

q: Histology of a vestibular nerve sheath tumor shows compact spindle cells in palisades around acellular zones. These palisaded whorls, giving the classic 'banana' appearance, are called?
ex: Verocay bodies in Antoni A regions mark the schwannoma; Antoni B areas are loose and myxoid.

q: Bent and Kuhn have proposed major diagnostic criteria for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis. Which of the following is NOT a classical accepted major criterion?
ex: Bent-Kuhn major criteria include elevated serum IgE, allergy mucin, nasal polyps, CT double density and positive fungal smear/culture — not IgA.

q: Suspicion of cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea arises after trauma with clear unilateral nasal drip. Which laboratory protein is essentially specific for confirming CSF?
ex: Beta-2 (tau) transferrin, sialic-acid-deficient transferrin found only in CSF, is a highly specific marker.

q: A patient with moderate asthma, bilateral allergic nasal polyps and aspirin-induced exacerbation of both is demonstrating which classic syndrome?
ex: Samter (ASA) triad = aspirin sensitivity + nasal polyposis + asthma; also called aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.

q: Which nasal infection presents as a pedunculated friable, vascular polypoid mass studded with whitish spore-bearing cysts, classically resembling a strawberry, caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi?
ex: Rhinosporidiosis shows strawberry-like intranasal polypoids with sporangiospores; treatment is surgical excision, and recurrence is common.

q: A patient with a grey-white thicker pseudomembrane over the fauces extending to the larynx and stridor. Which intervention cancels the damaging toxin quickly?
ex: Diphtheria antitoxin (IV, given earlier more effective) neutralizes circulating toxin; antibiotics only kill the organism.

q: This aggressive cellulitis of the submandibular space bilaterally elevates the floor of the mouth and larynx, trismus absent, with imminent airway risk. What is the best immediate priority?
ex: Ludwig's angina is a bilateral submandibular space infection that can precipitate airway obstruction; management begins with airway protection.

q: A neonate-young toddler with acute stiff neck, high fever, muffled cry and bulging of the posterior pharyngeal wall has an abscess. Infectious-inflammation usually develops at this age too because...
o: Infected lymph node behind prevertebral fascia in young children
Congenital cysts of the sinus pyrrhana
ex: Retropharyngeal abscess is mainly in children under 3 years from suppurative retropharyngeal lymphadenitis, which atrophies later.

q: The chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve, crossing behind the tympanic membrane inside the middle ear, carries which sensation?
o: Taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue
ex: Chorda tympani supplies special gustatory taste to the anterior 2/3 of tongue and secretomotor fibers to submandibular and sublingual glands.

q: Severe ear pain with vesicles over the pinna and concha and ipsilateral facial nerve paralysis following reactivation of Varicella-zoster. The name given is?
ex: Ramsay Hunt syndrome = herpes zoster oticus with geniculate ganglionitis: otagic, ear vesicles, facial palsy (may add VIII nerve deficits).

q: Glue-like non-infectious effusion behind an intact tympanic membrane in a toddler is the most common cause of which pattern of disability?
ex: Otitis media with effusion (glue ear) causes conductive hearing loss, borderline speech-language delay in preschool children.

q: A 70-year-old, symmetrical gradually worsening hearing, trouble understanding speech in noise, asking repetition; tympanogram undermines intact; audiogram reveals what profile?
ex: Presbycusis: bilateral, symmetric, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with preserved low tones and poor speech discrimination.

q: For the idiopathic peripheral facial nerve (Bell) palsy seen within 72 hours of onset, what is the recommended first line specific therapy?
ex: Early oral corticosteroids improve the recovery of Bell palsy; antivirals are sometimes added but are no substitute.

q: An aminoglycoside antibiotic given locally into the middle ear produces more selective harm to the vestibular apparatus than to hearing, leading to ataxia. Which one?
ex: Gentamicin is preferentially vestibulotoxic, a property used therapeutically to ablate vestibular function in Meigne; aminosynchronics damage the cochlea.

q: Keratoma of the lateral auditory canal: keratin plug against an intact diaphragm, bowing the wall and commonly associated with sinuso-bronchopulmonary disease. Which is correct?
o: Condition known as keratosis obturans, association chronic sinusitis plus bronchiectasis
ex: Keratose obturans: desquamated lamellae plug in the meatal canal, may disappear the meatus, linked with broncopulmonary-sinus disease.

q: Sinonasal inverted papillomas are benign but locally aggressive; epidemiologically they are associated with which viral infections and an elevated rate of eventual malignancy in some?
ex: Inverted papilloma, common in adult, recurs and can dedifferentiate to squamous cell carcinoma; linked to low-risk HPV subtypes.

q: In acute otitis media with severe Oral tympanic membrane bulging and ear pain, which antibiotic is appropriate first-line in most regions?
ex: Oral amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day is first-line; amoxicillin-clavulanate when resistance / after recent beta-lactam exposure.

q: Moderate-to-severe seasonal allergic rhinopathy with sneezing and pruritic wateriness is best controlled by which primary medication?
ex: Intranasal topical steroids are the most effective single therapy for allergic rhinitis; anti-histamine is secondary.

q: Chronic discharging ear in a man with persistent retro-orbital pain and diplopia from sixth cranial nerve weakness, all fine. This triad of otorrhea, pain and CN VI = carries diagnosis of?
ex: Gradenigo syndrome: PE in chronic petrous apicitis — abducent (VI) palsy, ipsilateral retrobulbar pain and otorrhea.

q: A patient from unsafe CSOM with cold-chill, hectic remittent fever and rec-distended neck veins. Sigmoid tap is tender; pick the correct intracranial complication.
ex: Sigmoid sinus thrombosis arises from synchronous middle ear — spiky fever + headache, and the sigmoid is the more frequent event than ITS of an ear.

q: In posterior ethmoid cells that overlie, lie above or lateral the sphenoid sinus may endanger which structure?  The cells are called Onodi.

q: A child with congenital bilateral external atresia of ear canals and conductive loss — which bone conduction device exploits direct skull stimulation and works well?

q: A unilateral elevated choanal polyp in youth arising through and accessory ostium originating from the maxillary antitum. What is the identification?
ex: Antrochoanal 'Killian' polyp — unilateral maxillary origin, passes posteriorly to choana causing complete nasal obstruction, surgically removed with uncinectomy.

o: To the pharyngeal roof (adenoid) and around the tubal orifice
ex: Luschka's tonsil is the pharyngeal tonsil incorporated in Latin adenoid; Gerlach's tubual tonsil rings the Eustachian orifice.

q: A painful purulent ear drainage in an older, diabetic individual whose granulation tissue at the canal floor bone is exposed. The most probable bacteria culture?
ex: Malignant (skull base/necrotic) otitis externa nearly always Pseudomonas aeruginosa in elderly diabetics; treatment is antipseudomonal.

q: A severe right snuffle with high-tone loss. Rinne response from the impaired side paradoxically is negative although there's marked sensorineural impairment. What is this exam memory artifact?

q: Sudden unilateral sensorineural within 3 weeks, unexplained, diagnostic primitivity calls for early intervention with what?
ex: Idiophytic sudden SNHL — early systemic corticosteroid as soon as feasible, impressively if within 3–14 days.

q: Which runs of facial nerve traverses between its geniculate and fallopian (the middle ear medial) and blends with the stapedius?

ex: The facial nerve's tympanic (horizontal) segment courses along the medial wall of middle ear and is at risk in cholesteatoma surgery.

q: In otitis media complications the most common site of intracranial cerebro-inthecotic abscess arising for the middle ear spread is the?

q: Disgusting in elderly with hypertension given posterior nasal bleeding that drips posteriorly. Which plexus has primary importance / site of bleeding?
o: Woodruff's plexus on the posterior-inferior edge of the lateral septum
ex: Posterior and elderly epistaxis usually arises from Woodruff's plexus — posterior and inferior of lateral nasal wall — often needs posterior packing.

q: What otological sign arises from a cholesteatoma eroding the horizontal semicircular canal?

q: Intestinal enterocytes form apoB48 from the same gene that gives hepatic apoB100. This arises mainly because of which process?

q: A patient with cholestatic jaundice. When the van den Bergh test is run in aqueous solution without alcohol, the expected finding is:
o: Prompt direct (immediate) reaction due to conjugated bilirubin
Only an indirect reaction, needing alcohol for colour
No colour generation under any condition
Colour that appears only in strong alkali

ex: NH3 + α-ketoglutarate (via glutamate dehydrogenase) → glutamate then glutamine traps ammonia.

q: Neonate with cataracts, hepatomegaly and vomiting; Benedict's test on urine is positive though glucose-oxidase strips are negative. The defective enzyme is:
ex: GALT (transferasase) deficiency = classic galactosemia; galactitol from aldose-reductase causes cataract.

q: An infant with a doll-like facies, single fasting hypoglycemia, lactate accumulation and gross hepatomegaly. Glycogen storage disease due to:
ex: Type Ia/mL (von Gierke) = glucose-6-phosphatase; severe fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acid + hepatomegaly.

q: An infant with severe hypotonia and an enlarged heart; glycogen piles up inside lysosomes. Deficient enzyme is:
ex: Type II (Pompe) is the only lysosomal GSD — acid maltase — affection, present with cardiomegaly.

q: A young man gets painful muscle cramps during strenuous exercise; an ischemic forearm test fails to produce lactate rise in venous blood. This matches deficiency of:
ex: McArdle type V = myophosphorylase; muscle cannot mobilize glycogen → gap in lactate + rhabdomyolysis.

q: Exercise-intolerance myopathy coexisting with hemolytic anemia points to a glycogenosis caused by a defect in:
ex: Tarui = type VII PFK-1 deficiency — RBC glycolysis stalls → hemolysis; white-muffice contracture.

q: By the age of 6-8 months this infant shows startle, regression and a cherry-red spot; hexosaminidase A is reduced. The accumulating substance is:
ex: Tay-Sachs = hexosaminidase A defect → GM2 ganglioside accumulates in neurons; cherry-red macula.

q: Chronic course with hepatosplenomegaly, bone crises and marrow Gaucher cells (tissue-paper cytoplasm). Deficient enzyme:
ex: Gaucher disease = β-glucocerebrosidase; glucocerebroside accumulates in macrophages.

q: Child with gargan boutons, cloudy cornea, organomegaly and peripheral neuropathy; alpha-l-iduronidase activity is near zero. Which molecules are trapped in cells?
ex: HIurler (MPS I) = α-L-iduronidase; also stores dermatane/heparan sulfate GAGs.

q: Darkening urine upon standing together with ochre deposits in the sclera and cartilages connote a defect in:
ex: Alkaptonuria = homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase defect; ochronosis polograms irreversible late arthropathy.

q: A youth has recurrent renal colic; urine sediment shows flat hexagonal crystals. The diagnosis is based on:
o: Defective renal tube transport of the dibasic (dibasic amino acid transport) group
ex: Cystauria: shared transport of cystine, ornithine, lysine & arginine fails; cystine stones crystals hexagonal.

q: Child with extreme hyperphenylalaninemia whose phenylalanine hydroxylase protein is present and functional. Which missing cofactor explains the picture?
ex: Biopterin (BH4) is hydroxylase cofactor; BH4-deficient hyperphenylene reproduces PKU phenotype.

q: Maple-syrup flavoured urine and neuro decline in a neonate stem from a deficiency of which enzymatic complex?
ex: MSUD = BCKD loss → Leu/Ile/Val and their keto-acids accumulate; low threshold: trefoil urine smell.

q: A classic deficiency where rash (dermatitis) in sun-exposed areas, diarrhea and memory of mood disturbance coexist is due to lack of:
ex: Pellagra (4 D's — dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia ) is niacin deficiency; Hartnup blocks tryptophan uptake.

q: RBC transketolase activity with/without added TPP is the standard functional assay for the reserve of which vitamin?
ex: Erythrocyte transketolase (TPP-dependent) activation index measures thiamine stores.

q: Perifollicular hemorrhages, bruise-prone gums, lusterless hair and marrow failure in a patient surviving on a bread-only diet — which hydroxylation will fail biochemically?
ex: Ascorbate (vit C) feb cococlear for prolyl/lysyl hydroxylases — failed collagen maturation → scurvy.

q: Bleeding tendency with a prolonged prothrombin time that recovers fully after a dose of vitamin K. The vitamin enables which chemical change directly?
ex: Vitamine K carboxylase glutamates → γ-carboxyglutamate (Gla), needed for factors II,VII,IX,X.

q: Father died of early MI; tendon xanthomas and very high LDL suggest a genetic loss-of-function of which protein?
ex: Familial hyperch Ch = LDLR defect → LDL clearance fails; statins to cut hepatic synthesis.

q: Most statins achieve their cholesterol-lowering effect by inhibiting a rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis — which one?
ex: HMG-CoA reductase is the RLE and target of statins; overwhelmed by context of nexin feedback.

q: A neonate with hemolytic crisis and near-zero ATP in RBCs; the defective enzyme is the one that phosphorylates PEP to pyruvate:

q: In which enzyme-deficient lactosis does biotin usually rescue the clinical picture (biotin supplement is beneficial)?
ex: Pyruvate carboxylase (biotin-dependent) is the gluconeogenic anaplerosis; its defect → biotin-responsive lactic acid.

q: Regular physical activity recruiting GLUT4 from vesicles to the sarcolemma is an insulin-independent component of the effect of:
